# Agentic Code Quality: Tools, Patterns, and Evidence for LLM-Generated Python Code
# Generated By: Claude Code (Claude Opus 4.6)

## What This Research Answers

LLM-based coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Aider) generate code with measurable quality risks: 1.7x more issues per PR, ~48% growth in duplicate code, and practitioner concerns about accelerated technical debt. This research identifies what tools, patterns, and evidence exist to address these risks for Python codebases. Five parallel discovery agents investigated testing discipline, duplicate detection, quality evaluation, parallel implementation, and integration patterns across 44 sources (23 deep-fetched, 21 snippet-level, 10 corrections identified during verification).

## Key Findings

| Pillar | What Exists | What Is Missing | Top Recommendation |
|--------|------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Testing Discipline** | TDD enforcement via hooks (tdd-guard) and prompts (superpowers); agentic PBT finding real bugs in NumPy [6]; mutation testing at Meta scale [9] | No controlled study comparing TDD-enforced vs non-TDD agentic code quality | Install tdd-guard for mechanical TDD enforcement; layer with prompt-level superpowers for defense in depth |
| **Duplicate Detection** | Ruff ~75 anti-reinvention rules [21]; Refurb stdlib checks [22]; jscpd cross-file clones [23]; academic tools for Type 1-3 clones | No "reinvented wheel" detector for third-party library reimplementation; no off-the-shelf semantic clone pipeline | Enable Ruff SIM+C4+PTH + Refurb in pre-commit; add jscpd to CI |
| **Quality Evaluation** | Self-Refine [1], Reflexion [2], CriticGPT [4]; configurable AI review tools (CodeRabbit, Qodo Merge) | No tool has built-in YAGNI/necessity detection -- the biggest gap across all pillars | Add custom necessity/proportionality instructions to CLAUDE.md and review tool configurations |
| **Parallel Implementation** | Best-of-N well-established (Agentless at $0.70/instance [5]); 16-parallel-Claude C compiler [13]; git worktree isolation [19] | No production piece-wise merge (best chunks from N candidates); no empirical cost-quality curve | Use git worktrees for parallel implementation on high-stakes changes; best-of-N with test-based selection |
| **Integration** | Claude Code 26 hook events [14]; Fowler's harness engineering framework [15]; hooks enforce deterministically where CLAUDE.md cannot | No published evidence comparing gate orderings; no benchmark for optimal layering | Order gates fast/cheap first (linters in PreToolUse) to expensive later (mutation testing in CI) |

## Decision Framework: 5 Steps to Improve LLM Code Quality

1. **Add deterministic static gates.** Enable Ruff (SIM+C4+PTH) and Refurb in pre-commit or PreToolUse hooks — these are fast, free, deterministic, and catch the most common LLM reinvention patterns. Add jscpd for cross-file clone detection (false-positive rate unpublished; tune thresholds per project).

2. **Enforce TDD mechanically.** Install tdd-guard as a PreToolUse hook to block implementation code without failing tests. Prompt-level enforcement (superpowers, CLAUDE.md) is complementary but bypassable.

3. **Add necessity evaluation to review.** No tool does this automatically. Write custom CLAUDE.md instructions or CodeRabbit/Qodo Merge rules that ask: "Is this code proportional to the requirement? Does it reinvent something available in a well-known library?"

4. **Layer sensors by cost.** Follow Fowler's "Keep Quality Left" [15]: fast linters first (ms), then tests (seconds), then mutation testing and broad review (minutes). Claude Code hooks map directly: PreToolUse for blocking gates, PostToolUse for observational sensors.

5. **Use parallel implementation for high-stakes work.** For complex changes, generate N candidates in isolated git worktrees and select the best via test results or LLM evaluation. Model diversity (cross-family) outperforms same-model parallelism [10].
